title: Exceptions and error contracts
summary: An exception is part of a function's interface, not an accident that happens to it. Deciding which exceptions a function raises, which it translates, and which it lets pass through is design work, and `except Exception: pass` is the decision to have no contract at all.
definition: An exception is an instance of a class deriving from `BaseException`, raised to abandon the current execution path and unwind the stack until a matching `except` clause is found. The unwinding runs `finally` blocks and context-manager `__exit__` methods on the way out, and the traceback records the frames it passed through.
purpose: Every function has two ways to finish, and only one of them is usually designed. Callers need to know what can go wrong in order to handle it: a retry loop needs to distinguish a timeout from a validation failure, and an HTTP layer needs to know which failures are the client's fault. Getting this right is also the difference between a traceback that names the cause and a log line saying `None` where an object was expected, three layers away from where the error actually happened.

body.md:
Python's control flow around exceptions has five clauses, and the two people forget are the useful ones:

```python
try:
    result = risky()
except TimeoutError as exc:      # narrowest first; ordering is top-down
    ...
except OSError:                   # TimeoutError is a subclass, so order matters
    ...
else:
    # runs only if no exception; keeps the try block down to the risky line
    use(result)
finally:
    # always runs: normal exit, exception, return, break
    release()
```

`else` exists so that the `try` block contains only the statement that can fail. Putting `use(result)` inside `try` means an unrelated `TimeoutError` raised by `use` is caught by the handler written for `risky`, which is how a handler ends up lying about what failed.

Because `except` clauses are tested in order and match subclasses, a broad clause above a narrow one makes the narrow one dead code, and unlike most dead code, this kind changes behaviour silently.

body.title: `except Exception: pass` is where outages come from
body.md:
It converts a loud failure into a quiet wrong answer. The job reports success, the metric stays green, and the missing rows are discovered a week later by someone reconciling totals.

If you must catch broadly (at a task boundary, a request handler, a plugin call site), then log with `exc_info=True`, record a failure metric, and re-raise or return an explicit error value. The rule worth internalising: catch an exception only when you can either fix the situation or add information. Otherwise let it travel.

Also note `except Exception` deliberately does *not* catch `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit`, because those derive from `BaseException` directly. `except BaseException` (or a bare `except:`) catches them, which is how a worker becomes unkillable by Ctrl-C.

body.caption: Chaining: `raise ... from` is what keeps the cause in the traceback
body.expected_output: ConfigError | retries must be an integer, got 'lots' | caused by ValueError

body.md:
Chaining is the mechanism behind "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred". If you raise inside an `except` block, Python sets `__context__` automatically and prints both. Writing `from exc` sets `__cause__` instead, which changes the wording to "The above exception was the direct cause" and states that the relationship is intentional. `from None` suppresses the chain entirely, appropriate when the inner error is an implementation detail the caller must not depend on, and inappropriate when someone will have to debug it at 3am.

The practical rule for layering: translate at boundaries and preserve the cause. A repository turning `asyncpg.UniqueViolationError` into `AlreadyExists` gives its callers a stable contract; doing it without `from exc` throws away the constraint name that says *which* uniqueness failed.

sources.locator: PEP 3134: Exception Chaining and Embedded Tracebacks

body.caption: Reading a traceback: bottom-up, and the last frame is rarely the bug
body.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app/handlers.py", line 42, in create_user
    profile = build_profile(payload)          # <- your code: start here
  File "app/profiles.py", line 17, in build_profile
    return Profile(name=payload["name"])     # <- the failing statement
KeyError: 'name'                              # <- the type and its argument

# Read: the innermost frame is where it surfaced; the *cause* is usually the
# frame above it that passed bad data. 'name' is the missing key, so the
# question is which caller built a payload without it.

body.title: Designing a function's error contract
steps: List the ways this function can fail that a caller could plausibly respond to differently. That list is the contract.
Give each one a type: a stdlib exception when the meaning matches exactly, otherwise a subclass of one project-level base exception.
Document them in the docstring. An undocumented raise is a bug the caller will find in production.
Translate foreign exceptions at the boundary with `raise MyError(...) from exc`, so the driver's types never reach callers.
Let everything else propagate. Unexpected exceptions are information, and catching them destroys it.
Put cleanup in `finally` or a context manager. Never rely on the happy path to release a resource.

body.definition_md: `ExceptionGroup` (3.11+) carries several unrelated exceptions raised concurrently, the normal outcome when a `TaskGroup` has multiple failing children. `except*` matches by type *within* the group and can handle some members while re-raising the rest, which plain `except` cannot express.

body.title: What operators need from your exceptions
body.md:
A message that identifies the specific instance, not the category. `"config invalid"` costs a debugging session; `"config key 'retries' must be an integer, got 'lots'"` costs nothing.

Also: never put secrets in an exception message, because messages end up in logs, error trackers and sometimes HTTP responses. Sanitise at the raise site: a connection error that includes the DSN has just written the password to your log aggregator.

And keep the mapping to HTTP status codes in one place. Scattering `except ValueError: return 400` through handlers means the twentieth handler will disagree with the first.

components.name: exception class
components.role: The type; what `except` matches on and the primary signal to the caller.

components.name: message / args
components.role: The instance-specific detail that makes a log line actionable.

components.name: __cause__ / __context__
components.role: The chain. `from exc` sets the cause explicitly; raising inside a handler sets context automatically.

components.name: traceback
components.role: The frames the exception unwound through; the reading order is bottom-up.

components.name: finally / __exit__
components.role: Cleanup that runs during unwinding, which is the only cleanup you can rely on.

common_errors.error: A failure disappears: the job logs success, but rows are missing.
common_errors.cause: `except Exception: pass`, or a handler that logs at DEBUG and continues.
common_errors.fix: Catch only what you can act on. When a broad catch is structurally necessary, log with `exc_info=True`, count a failure metric, and re-raise or return an explicit error.

common_errors.error: A narrow `except TimeoutError` clause never fires.
common_errors.cause: A broader clause (`except OSError`) is listed above it, and clauses are tested in order with subclass matching.
common_errors.fix: Order handlers narrowest-first. If two are unrelated, order does not matter, but check the hierarchy before assuming they are.

common_errors.error: A worker cannot be stopped with Ctrl-C, or exits with the wrong status code.
common_errors.cause: A bare `except:` or `except BaseException:` swallowing `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`.
common_errors.fix: `except Exception:` for application errors. Only catch `BaseException` to run cleanup, and always re-raise.

common_errors.error: A production traceback ends at your own wrapper exception with no sign of the real cause.
common_errors.cause: `raise MyError(str(exc))` discards the chain; `from None` suppresses it deliberately.
common_errors.fix: `raise MyError(...) from exc`. Reserve `from None` for cases where the inner error genuinely must not leak.

common_errors.error: A `return` inside `try` appears to be overridden, or an exception vanishes without a handler.
common_errors.cause: A `return`, `break` or `continue` inside `finally` discards the in-flight exception and replaces the return value.
common_errors.fix: Keep `finally` to cleanup only. Never return or break from it.

common_errors.error: `TypeError: catching classes that do not inherit from BaseException is not allowed`.
common_errors.cause: `except (ValueError, "oops")` or catching an instance instead of a class, often a stray comma.
common_errors.fix: Catch a class or a tuple of classes. `except (ValueError, TypeError) as exc:`.

common_errors.error: An `except` clause runs but `exc` is undefined on the next line.
common_errors.cause: `as exc` is deleted at the end of the clause, deliberately, to avoid a reference cycle holding the whole frame.
common_errors.fix: Copy what you need out of the clause: `message = str(exc)` before leaving it.

best_practices: Catch the narrowest exception that lets you take a specific action, and let everything else propagate.
Give your project one base exception and derive domain errors from it, so callers can catch your failures without catching library bugs.
Always `raise ... from exc` when translating at a boundary; the cause is the most valuable part of the report.
Write messages that identify the instance (the key, the value, the id), not just the category.
Use `else` to keep the `try` block down to the statements that can actually fail.
Put every resource release in a context manager or `finally`, and never a `return` in `finally`.
Document raised exceptions in the docstring; treat an undocumented raise as an interface change.
production_considerations: Exception messages reach logs, error trackers and sometimes clients. Sanitise DSNs, tokens and PII at the raise site, not at the logging layer.
Map exceptions to HTTP status codes in one central handler. Duplicated per-route mapping drifts and produces inconsistent APIs.
Retries must key on exception type: a timeout is retryable, a validation error never is. This is the main reason a coarse error contract costs money.
`ExceptionGroup` from `asyncio.TaskGroup` means a single `except SomeError` may not fire even though `SomeError` occurred; concurrent code needs `except*`.
Exceptions in `__del__` and in generator finalisation are printed but not raised: cleanup logic that relies on them being caught will not work.
Raising in a hot loop is meaningfully slower than a conditional. Exceptions for control flow are idiomatic (`StopIteration`) but not free.
anti_patterns: `except Exception: pass`, and its cousin `except Exception: return None`.
`raise Exception("failed")`: untyped, uncatchable-by-meaning, and indistinguishable from a bug.
Using exceptions for expected outcomes a caller must handle every time (a lookup miss is better as `Optional`).
`assert` for validating untrusted input: assertions are removed under `python -O`.
Logging and re-raising at every level, which multiplies one failure into ten log entries.
